description: We're Nebula Collectors, a team mainly from Cumilla Collectorate School & College, Bangladesh, competing in the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. Our project, “Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data,” combines NASA Earth observation, climate, soil, and crop data with AI-powered guidance to help farmers assess crop suitability, plan rotations, manage water, improve soil health, and prepare for weather risks—supporting smarter, more resilient, and sustainable agriculture.
summary:
**Field Shift** is a bilingual (English/বাংলা) crop decision-support platform designed for Bangladeshi farmers. Farmers select their district and upazila to receive a seasonal shortlist of crops, ranked by estimated income, crop suitability, salinity tolerance, waterlogging risk, and water demand. Adjustable priority sliders let farmers personalize the ranking according to their needs.

The platform integrates Bangladesh Crop Zoning economic data, NASA POWER climate observations, and NASA OPERA DSWx-S1 satellite-based flood signals. It applies FAO-56 crop water demand calculations and the Maas–Hoffman salinity response model to support its assessments. A Live Field feature provides recent 14-day weather information, while an AI Copilot uses the farmer's location, crop rankings, priorities, and weather conditions to provide contextual assistance. A dedicated Data Sources page documents datasets, methodologies, and limitations.

Field Shift transforms complex Earth observation and agricultural data into understandable, location-specific crop recommendations. It aims to help smallholder farmers make more informed decisions amid increasing salinity, flooding, and unpredictable rainfall.
details:
What it does and how it works

Field Shift (built on the AgriSheba data project) helps Bangladeshi farmers choose crops. The farmer picks a district and upazila, or clicks the map. The app then ranks crops for each season (Rabi, Kharif-1, Kharif-2), and the ranking follows five priority sliders: income, salinity tolerance, waterlogging tolerance, water demand and crop suitability.

The scores come from real data:

  • Income: Crop Zoning gross margin and benefit–cost ratios.
  • Salinity: each crop’s Maas & Hoffman tolerance curve.
  • Water demand: FAO-56 crop evapotranspiration.
  • Waterlogging: NASA OPERA DSWx-S1 flood signals, checked against JRC permanent water.

A Live Field tab shows the last 14 days of NASA POWER weather. A Data Sources tab lists every dataset, method and limitation. The AI Copilot automatically receives the farmer’s location, ranking, priorities and live weather, so they don’t have to type it.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Farmers get location-specific, transparent advice instead of generic crop lists, and each score can be traced to its source.
  • The intended impact is better crop choices in places facing salinity, flooding and irregular rain, which means lower risk and better income for smallholders.
  • It makes NASA and FAO data usable by non-experts, in Bangla and English.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Languages: Python for data processing. JavaScript, HTML and CSS for the app, which is a single index.html file with no build step.
  • Python libraries: pandas, NumPy, SciPy, requests, xarray, h5netcdf, rasterio and the Earth Engine API. Jupyter notebooks were used for the IMERG rainfall and MODIS LSWI processing.
  • Data and services: Bangladesh Crop Zoning API, BAMIS, NASA POWER, MERRA-2, CERES, GPM IMERG, OPERA DSWx-S1, MODIS MOD09A1, JRC Global Surface Water, and Google Earth Engine.
  • Methods: FAO-56 Penman–Monteith and Maas & Hoffman salinity response.
  • Web tools: Leaflet with OpenStreetMap tiles for the map, a geocoding service to find coordinates for live weather, Google Fonts, and browser local storage for small settings.
  • AI: an external AI chat service powers the Copilot, and Claude (Anthropic) assisted with coding and testing.
  • Development: GitHub for version control and hosting, and headless-browser (Playwright) tests for layout and scoring.
  • Hardware: no specialised hardware. The app runs in any modern browser on phones and desktops. Please replace this line with your team’s actual setup if you want to be specific.

Creativity

It combines government crop economics, satellite flood signals and agronomic models into one slider-driven ranking. The AI Copilot adds this context automatically, and the whole app is bilingual.

Factors the team considered

  • Data limits: salinity is only a recorded label per upazila, not a lab measurement. Water demand is a simplified seasonal estimate. Where data is missing, crops are not penalized.
  • Honesty: satellite and model values are shown as indicators, not field measurements. There is no yield-validation dataset yet, so advice should be confirmed with local agricultural officers.
  • Access: the app works on mobile and in Bangla, and as a single file it is simple to host.
